messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: overdispersed multinomial
parts:
Hi,

I am asking for advice on the following problem: I am modelling
3-dimensional count data (time use survey, 10-minute blocks). I have
some variables, call them x, that predict means after a transformation
(at least that's what the model we have says), so I am simulating it as

data {
int<lower=0> N_worker;
real<lower=0> x[N_worker];
int<lower=0> lhm_tmb[N_worker,3]; // leisure, home, market; timeblocks
}
parameters {
real<lower=0,upper=1> alpha;
real<lower=0,upper=1-alpha> beta;
}
transformed parameters {
real<lower=0,upper=1> hs;
real<lower=0,upper=1> ls;
hs <- beta;
ls <- 1-alpha-beta;
}
model {
for (i in 1:N_worker) {
vector[3] lhm;
real lshare;
real hshare;
lshare <- ls*(x[i]+1)/(1+x[i]*(ls+hs));
hshare <- hs*(x[i]+1)/(1+x[i]*(ls+hs));
lhm[1] <- lshare;
lhm[2] <- hshare;
lhm[3] <- 1-lshare-hshare;
lhm_tmb[i] ~ multinomial(lhm);
}
}

This works, but posterior predictive checks fail on variances (and
possibly correlations) of lhm_tmb.

I tried overdispersion with a Dirichlet distribution, which improves
matters, but since it is only one extra degree of freedom, two of the
variances are still not close (and this is a moment we care about).

Are there any other mean-preserving ways of overdispersing multinomial
that have more degrees of freedom?

Best,

Tamas

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] overdispersed multinomial
parts:
Instead of Dirichlet you can use rescaled lognormals. For a direct comparison of Dirichlet with rescaled lognormals, see section 6.1 of this paper:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/moments.pdf

For more on that particular example see the expressions in the lower-left on page 1403 in this paper:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/bois2.pdf

A
